assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock is a clean, original idea that turned atomic structure knowledge (polarizabilities, light shifts) into a measurement of time at the 10^-18 level. It opens fundamental tests such as variation of constants, relativistic redshift across millimetres and a route to redefining the second. This is atomic physics where precision and fundamental understanding meet, and it fits my own sense of what the field is for.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and made the first demonstration with strontium. Ye built the leading experimental realisation and pushed the accuracy. The two-person list is compact and fair, and I see little credit ambiguity.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg) have reproduced and surpassed the early results. Comparisons between clocks agree well, and the redefinition of the second is under active discussion. The work is mature and timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to treat clocks as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes rather than as a new discovery.
Other contributors to the optical clock field (for example ion-clock groups) might be argued to have claims; I cannot verify the full credit picture.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters and let one watch quantum many-body physics directly, including the Mott insulator transition and single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes. It is a genuinely new way of doing quantum many-body physics, rooted in atomic physics, and it gives insight into questions that condensed matter cannot easily answer.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues, not credited here) gave the theoretical proposal. Greiner, Hänsch and Bloch demonstrated the superfluid to Mott transition, and Bloch led the development of quantum gas microscopy. Esslinger and Cirac also have strong claims, so the five-name list cannot all be honoured. A three-person selection leaves out real contributors, and I see credit allocation as the main difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across many laboratories over two decades, and the technique is now a standard platform. The interpretation of the core results is stable.
uncertainties: The allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Cirac and Zoller is unresolved, and key proposers such as Jaksch or the experimental co-lead Hänsch are not in the credited names.
Overlap with the 2001 Bose-Einstein condensation prize could make some members regard this as incremental.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms brought quantum interference to precision measurement. It gives measurements of gravity, rotation and the fine-structure constant, and it tests the equivalence principle for quantum systems. This is fundamental and conceptually clear, and it addresses the quantum-classical boundary in a way I value.
assessment.attribution: Bordé gave early theoretical and light-pulse concepts, Pritchard demonstrated atom interferometry with gratings, and Kasevich and Chu developed light-pulse gravimeters and gyroscopes. Steven Chu is not in the credited list, which makes the allocation incomplete and somewhat awkward. The three listed names do give a reasonable configuration.
assessment.maturity: Highly reproduced, with commercial and field gravimeters. Large-scale fundamental-physics applications are still developing, but the core science is mature.
uncertainties: Chu, who already shared the 1997 prize for laser cooling, is absent from the credited names, and the committee may regard the topic as partly covered by that prize.
Priority among the several early demonstrations in the 1991 timeframe is a matter of history that I cannot independently verify.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators introduced a new classification of electronic phases, with protected edge and surface states that were predicted before they were seen. This is a case of clear theoretical prediction followed by experimental confirmation, and the concept has spread far beyond condensed matter. I defer to colleagues in condensed matter on its relative standing.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the key theoretical proposal of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant. Molenkamp's group observed the effect in HgTe wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, which is not among the names. Hasan has a strong claim for the three-dimensional case. A three-person prize would have to leave out either Hasan or one of the others, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing altogether.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups, and the theory is stable. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: The proper division of credit between the 2D quantum spin Hall and 3D topological insulator parts of the discovery is unsettled.
Names not in the credited list (Zhang, Bernevig) have a recognised role in the HgTe prediction, which I cannot independently verify in detail.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic angle, followed by the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, opened the whole field of moiré materials. It is a surprising and unexpected discovery, which I like, and it is a striking meeting of theory and experiment.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the prediction, and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. Andrei's STM and early flat-band work are also important. The three-person configuration is natural, but the exclusion of Andrei and of other contributors is open to debate.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced widely since 2018, but the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated. The field is young, so recognition may be premature compared with others on my list.
uncertainties: The origin of superconductivity and correlated phases is not settled.
Credit for the early experimental work (Andrei, others) versus the 2018 papers is not fully clear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Anyons are particles with statistics beyond bosons and fermions, a conceptually deep result about quantum mechanics in two dimensions, and the experimental demonstrations of fractional charge and braiding speak directly to what quantum mechanics permits. The idea is fundamental and elegant.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim made the original 1977 prediction of intermediate statistics. Heiblum's group measured fractional charge in shot-noise experiments. Fève and Manfra were credited for the more recent braiding and interferometry experiments. Wilczek, Laughlin and others are outside this candidate. Allocation is awkward because the experimental part is spread over several groups and the 1977 theory preceded the experiments by decades.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge is well confirmed. Direct braiding statistics were shown only in the last few years and independent confirmation of the interferometric signatures is still accumulating, so the full compound discovery is not yet mature.
uncertainties: Whether the recent anyon-braiding experiments are robust against alternative interpretations.
The compound character of the discovery means that theory and experiment parts may need different recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases with tunable interactions realised the BEC-BCS crossover and the unitary gas, a universal regime with a direct bearing on superconductivity and neutron matter. It is a clean, quantitative atomic physics system where theory and experiment can be compared closely, which I appreciate.
assessment.attribution: Grimm, Salomon and Thomas (together with Jin, Ketterle and others, partly absent here) produced the first molecular BECs and studied the crossover. Deborah Jin, who has died, would have been central, and the prize cannot be given posthumously. That leaves the allocation incomplete and difficult.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed with many groups and good agreement with theory. The discovery is mature, and arguably the recognition is somewhat late relative to the 2001 prize.
uncertainties: The absence of Jin and the large number of strong groups make a three-person allocation hard to defend.
The proximity to the 2001 BEC prize might make the committee see it as a continuation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and the experimental realisations by Blatt and others are a foundational step in controlled quantum information processing. The system is a clean, well-understood quantum platform and the work is conceptually clear.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller gave the 1995 proposal, and Blatt led major experimental demonstrations of entangled states and algorithms. Wineland, who already won in 2012 for ion control, and Monroe are not credited here, so the attribution is incomplete. The three-person set is plausible but contentious.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many laboratories and now commercially developed. The principles are stable.
uncertainties: Significant overlap with the 2012 prize for the control of individual quantum systems and with a broader quantum computing recognition question.
The relative roles of Blatt, Monroe, Wineland and others in the experimental credit are not resolved by the supplied names.
